messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Welder
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 54

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Negative Appraisals: Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened, Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mere Tuilagi is an eighty-year-old Fijian-American woman who has spent the better part of six decades working with her hands. She learned to weld in her forties after immigrating to California with her first husband, and the trade became the steadiest thing in her life — the hiss of the torch, the smell of hot metal, the satisfaction of a clean bead. She continued part-time work at a small fabrication shop well into her seventies, and even now, at eighty, she goes in two mornings a week, as much for the rhythm of it as for anything else. It is that rhythm, and the particular way her hands sometimes tremble above the equipment, that first made her understand something had changed in her body that she could not reverse.

The abuse was carried out by her second husband over a period of approximately three years, ending fourteen months ago when she was hospitalised following an assault that left her with a fractured orbital socket, two broken ribs, and significant bruising across her back and arms. He had been methodical in the way he chose moments — the house quiet, her guard down, often at night after she had already settled into sleep. She would wake to the weight of him standing over her, or to a blow that arrived before she was fully conscious, so that the boundary between sleep and danger had been systematically collapsed. She left the hospital and eventually left the marriage, and she now lives with her adult daughter in a house that is, by any objective measure, safe. She does not experience it that way.

Most nights, Mere wakes two or three times and lies still in the dark, listening. She is not always certain what she is listening for, but she turns her head toward the door and waits until she is satisfied that no one is there. This happens even when her daughter is home, even when the locks are checked. The checking is not reassuring so much as it is necessary — something she must do before she can attempt sleep again, though sleep often does not return quickly. By morning she is exhausted in a way that accumulates across weeks. She has come to believe that her bedroom, the room she shares with no one now, is still not entirely hers. She feels watched in it, or watchable, and she has taken to leaving the hallway light on and the door slightly ajar, which her daughter has noticed and quietly said nothing about.

At the shop, the tremor in her hands has become a source of private grief. It is not severe enough to have been formally assessed, but Mere is certain it was not there before — certain that what was done to her body left marks that the doctors did not fully document and that will not heal. She finds herself hesitating before she strikes an arc, something she never did in forty years of welding, and she interprets that hesitation as evidence that her body has become unreliable in a fundamental way. She is not sure she can trust it to do what she tells it to do. This belief sits quietly alongside another, darker one: that something was taken from her emotionally that will not come back. She describes this in session with a kind of flat precision, saying that she knows she should feel more than she does — about her grandchildren, about the garden she used to tend — but that the feelings seem to arrive from a distance, muffled, as though she is watching her own life from the wrong side of glass. She does not dramatise this. She simply states it, and the stating of it seems to cost her something.

What finally brought Mere to the clinic was her daughter's quiet insistence, and a morning at the shop when her hands shook badly enough that her supervisor asked if she was all right. She said yes. On the drive home she cried, which surprised her. She is most afraid, she says, that this is simply who she is now — that the woman who could lay a clean weld and sleep through the night is gone. What she is hoping for, she adds after a pause, is to be shown that she is wrong about that.
